what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Investors may choose the founder they can control
sections.para: Between two equal founders, my hypothesis is that investors pick the one they can steer, moving the founder towards commodity as labels did with performers. Research shows investors prefer coachable founders, contracts give them control and half of founders were gone as CEO by year three. Strong-minded, ethical founders are filtered out.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Investors select for coachability, which does not predict success
sections.para: Studying survivors makes unrelated practices look like causes. Investors prefer coachable founders, contracts give them control when performance is poor, and half of founders were no longer CEO by year three. Founder control lowers valuations, yet founder-led companies returned about three times more over 25 years.

sections.label: The survivors we study
sections.line: Studying only winners makes risky practices look successful
sections.para: Business writing copies winners and ignores those who did the same and failed. Jerker Denrell showed in 2003 that observed organisations are survivors, and that risky practices unrelated to performance can look positively related to it among them. The real question is why the winner was chosen and backed.

sections.label: Who is the commodity
sections.line: Labels made performers swappable; funds can do that too
sections.para: Songs, producers and distribution were often the real talent: the top ten producers made about 40% of top five hits in 2010 to 2014, against 19% in the late 1980s. K-pop's TVXQ case capped contracts at seven years. When a VC board member dies, startups fail more, so the network is the scarce asset.

sections.label: Why one and not the other
sections.line: Coachability is a polite word for controllability
sections.para: Given two equal founders, my hypothesis is that investors pick the one who will take direction and step aside. Nobody has tested that directly, but coachability sits close. Letwin and colleagues wrote in 2023 that investors prefer coachable entrepreneurs, though it does not necessarily make the firm more successful.

sections.label: Control is written into the contract
sections.line: Venture contracts design in investor control and founder replaceability
sections.para: Kaplan and Strömberg read 213 venture investments in 119 companies: investors get full control if the firm performs poorly and give most of it back if it does very well. Non-compete and vesting provisions make it more expensive for the founder to leave.

sections.label: Founders get replaced
sections.line: By year three, half the founders were not CEO
sections.para: Wasserman's study of 212 US startups found 50% of founders gone as CEO by year three, 40% remaining in year four and under 25% leading the IPO; most were shocked. Ewens and Marx count founder replacement in 15% of 11,929 firms, a lower figure in the same direction.

sections.label: Luck, place and timing
sections.line: Timing and place shape success as much as talent
sections.para: In the MusicLab experiment with 14,341 people, showing popularity made success more unequal and unpredictable. Moretti found the ten largest computer science clusters hold 69% of US inventors, and that inventors moving into a cluster produce more. Copying winners' moves does not reliably reproduce their results.

sections.label: The investors' answer, and the long run
sections.line: Control raises valuations, but founder-led firms win long term
sections.para: Founder control cuts pre-money valuation by 17.1 to 22.0 percent, and replacement can improve exits, but both measure the investor's value. Bain found founder-led S&P 500 firms returned 3.1 times more from 1990 to 2014. Investors' datasets also exclude founders who refused the terms, which is undersampling again.

sections.label: How to test it
sections.line: Three ways to test the controllability hypothesis
sections.para: Follow founders rated for coachability at the pitch for ten years, including what happened to users. Compare product direction, prices and ethics commitments in founder-replaced and founder-kept companies. Survey founders who refused term sheets: if they score higher on independence and lower on coachability, the filter is real.

sections.label: What this means for strong-minded founders
sections.line: Strong-minded founders should reach the big stick first
sections.para: Founders with strong vision and ethics are disadvantaged because investors correctly read them as hard to overrule; that describes many European founders. Tech's winner-takes-all markets are a partial exception. The advice is to gain leverage before needing money, which agents make more possible, as Sell, don't issue and The fork next door explore.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: No study tests controllability, and some evidence cuts against
sections.para: Coachability is only a proxy, and Wasserman and Ewens and Marx link replacement to better valuations and exits. Bain's figures are its own analysis, the tenure data is old and the music figures are industry analyses. Investors are not villains, and the founder writing this has a stake.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: the studies on founders, investors and luck
sections.para: Denrell 2003; Letwin and colleagues on coachability; Kaplan and Strömberg 2003; Wasserman 2008 and 2017; Ewens and Marx 2018; Ewens and Sosyura 2023; Bain 2026; Meta and Alphabet proxy statements; The Pudding; Salganik, Dodds and Watts 2006; and Moretti 2021. Drafted from a voice memo of 16 October 2026.
